Washington-on-the-Brazos is the capital of Republic of Texas. The Republic of Texas (Spanish: República de Tejas), or simply Texas, was a short-lived sovereign country in North America from March 2, 1836, to February 19, 1846.

Named in the opening chapters of Genesis, this figure is considered the first human aware of God across several Abrahamic faiths, and in Christian tradition, his sin in Eden introduced death into the world — who is he?
Adam is the name given in Genesis 1-5 to the first human.
The daughter of an Imperial Russian general, she served as People's Commissar for Welfare and became the first woman in history to sit in a national cabinet — who was this Bolshevik?
Alexandra Kollontai was Soviet politician and diplomat (1872–1952).
Once co-leader of Alliance 90/The Greens alongside Robert Habeck, she became Germany's foreign minister and then president of the UN General Assembly's 80th session — who is she?
Annalena Baerbock (born 15 December 1980) is a German diplomat and politician of the Alliance 90/The Greens party.
This 9th-century Iranian revolutionary's uprising was considered an offshoot of neo-Mazdakism and showed the enduring strength of pre-Islamic Persian identity in the region — who led it?

Babak Khorramdin (795 or 798 - January 838) was one of the main Iranian revolutionary leaders of the Iranian Khorram-Dinn ("Those of the joyous religion"), which was a local freedom movement fighting the Abbasid Caliphate.
Which former campaign manager for Hillary Clinton represented Brooklyn on the City Council before being elected mayor of New York City in 2013?
Bill de Blasio (born Warren Wilhelm Jr., May 8, 1961) is an American former politician who served as the 110th mayor of New York City from 2014 to 2021.
Having founded Turkey's first bank, İş Bankası, this politician went on to become prime minister under Atatürk and later the country's president throughout the 1950s — who is he?
Celâl Bayar (16 May 1883 - 22 August 1986) was a Turkish economist and politician who was the president of Turkey from 1950 to 1960.

This 8th-century Byzantine emperor exploited civil war in the Muslim world to press the Arab frontier, then resettled Christians in Thrace to tighten his grip on the Balkans against the Bulgars — who was he?
Constantine V (July 718 - 14 September 775) was Byzantine emperor from 741 to 775.
An American politician and businessman who served as the 46th vice president under George W. Bush from 2001 to 2009, considered the architect of the Iraq War—who was he?
Dick Cheney (January 30, 1941 - November 3, 2025) was an American politician and businessman who served as the 46th vice president of the United States under President George W. Bush.
A daughter of Peter the Great, she ruled from 1741 to 1762 and stayed beloved partly for a remarkable vow: not to execute a single person during her reign — which empress?
Elizabeth of Russia was Empress of Russia (1741–1762). During her reign Elizabeth continued the policies of her father and brought about a remarkable Age of Enlightenment in Russia.
The CEO of the ACS engineering group, this Spanish businessman is better known as the football boss who launched the 'Galácticos' policy of signing the world's best players — who is he?
Florentino Pérez (Spanish; born 8 March 1947) is a Spanish businessman and the president of football club Real Madrid, as well as chairman and CEO of ACS Group, a civil engineering company.
This Roman general and politician, adopted by his uncle Tiberius in AD 4, is best remembered for his campaigns against the German chieftain Arminius. Who was he?
Germanicus (24 May 15 BC - 10 October AD 19) was a Roman general and politician most famously known for his campaigns against Arminius in Germania.
Ascending the throne in 2020 after his cousin's death, this monarch became the fifteenth ruler of a dynasty that has led Oman since the 18th century — who is he?
Haitham bin Tariq (born 11 October 1955) is the Sultan and Prime Minister of Oman.

In the Book of Genesis, this son of Noah appears in the story of Noah's drunkenness and is later named ancestor of the peoples of the Aegean, Anatolia, and Greece — who is he?
Japheth was one of the three sons of Noah in the Book of Genesis.
This U.S. president assumed office in 1841 after his predecessor died just 31 days into his term, becoming the first vice president ever to ascend to the presidency this way — who is he?
John Tyler (March 29, 1790 - January 18, 1862) was the tenth president of the United States, serving from 1841 to 1845, after briefly holding office as the tenth vice president in 1841.
A former Director of Public Prosecutions, this Labour leader became the UK's Prime Minister in 2024 — who is he?
Keir Starmer (born 2 September 1962) is a British politician and former lawyer who has served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom since 2024 and as Leader of the Labour Party since 2020.
In Christian eschatology, this future event will see Jesus Christ return to sit on a "great white throne" and render a final verdict on every person who has ever lived — what is this event called?
Last Judgment is a central Christian eschatological event marking the return of Jesus Christ to evaluate all of humanity, both the living and the resurrected dead (Jn 5:28-29).

He fought in the Burma Campaign for the British Indian Army and retired a Pakistani colonel, then in 1971 became commander-in-chief and founder of a brand-new nation's armed forces — which four-star general was he?
M. A. G. Osmani (1 September 1918 - 16 February 1984) was a Bangladeshi military officer, revolutionary and politician.
Developed in the Soviet Union by Joseph Stalin, this communist ideology became the predominant state ideology across the Eastern Bloc during the Cold War. What is it?
Marxism–Leninism is a communist ideology that became the largest faction of the communist movement following the October Revolution.
Twice shot in the head and surviving both times, this Russian field marshal later defeated Napoleon's invasion using a strategy of attrition — who was he?
Mikhail Kutuzov was Field Marshal of the Russian Empire (1745–1813).
France's longest-serving head of state across 22 years, he was the country's second president and its very last monarch, deposed in 1870 — who was he?
Napoleon III (born Charles-Louis Napolon Bonaparte; 20 April 1808 - 9 January 1873) was President of France from 1848 to 1852 and then Emperor of the French from 1852 until his deposition in 1870.
Often shown as a nude woman covered in stars and arching protectively over the Earth, this Egyptian deity embodies the sky itself — who is she?
Nut (goddess) (Ancient), also known by various other transcriptions, is the goddess of the sky, stars, cosmos, mothers, astronomy, and the universe in the ancient Egyptian religion.
He started out as a care officer for Camden Council before his drag character Lily Savage made him a household name on British television — which performer was he?
Paul O'Grady (14 June 1955 - 28 March 2023) was an English drag queen, comedian, broadcaster, actor, and writer.
Established by Hitler on 16 March 1939, the day after German troops occupied the Czech rump state, this partially annexed Nazi territory was home mostly to ethnic Czechs — what was it called?
Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia was a partially annexed territory of Nazi Germany that was established on 16 March 1939 after the German occupation of the Czech lands.
Founder of the System Capital Management investment group, this billionaire is both Ukraine's richest man and the owner of football club Shakhtar Donetsk — who is he?
Rinat Akhmetov (born 21 September 1966) is a Ukrainian oligarch, billionaire and businessman.

A hero of the Texas Revolution, this statesman served as both the first and third president of the Republic of Texas, and is the only American ever elected governor of two different states. Who was he?
Sam Houston (March 2, 1793 - July 26, 1863) was an American military general and statesman who played a prominent role in the Texas Revolution.
This Indian politician has served two separate terms as Chief Minister of Karnataka, and was only the second person ever to complete a full five-year term in that office — who is he?

Siddaramaiah (born 3 August 1947), also referred to by his nickname Siddu, is an Indian politician, lawyer, former lecturer and statesman who served as the 16th Chief Minister of Karnataka from 2013 to 2018 and 2023 to 2026.
Before becoming French prime minister in 2025, this Renaissance party politician held ministerial posts covering local authorities, overseas territories, and the armed forces — who is he?
Sébastien Lecornu (French; born 11 June 1986) is a French politician who has served as Prime Minister of France since September 2025.

Recognized only by the Soviet Union and Mongolia, this partially-recognized socialist state in North Asia existed for 23 years before its parliament requested absorption into the Russian SFSR in 1944 — what was it, whose territory now forms a namesake region of Russia?
Tuvan People's Republic (TPR), known simply as Tuva, was a partially recognized socialist republic that existed between 1921 and 1944 in North Asia.

This German Generalfeldmarschall (1891–1945) began as a hard-driving panzer commander but became known as a practitioner of defensive warfare. He gained Hitler's attention early and commanded the Ninth Army in 1941–1942 — who is he?
Walter Model (24 January 1891 - 21 April 1945) was a German Generalfeldmarschall during World War II.

Founded in London in 1844 by George Williams, this now-global youth organization serves over 64 million people across 120 countries and promotes healthy body, mind, and spirit development — name the organization?
YMCA is a worldwide youth organization based in Vernier, Canton of Geneva, Switzerland, with more than 64 million beneficiaries in 120 countries.
A grandson of caliph Abu Bakr and the first child born to Islam's earliest converts, he led a rival caliphate based in Mecca during the Second Fitna until his death in 692 — who was he?
Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr: Arab leader of Mecca-based caliphate from 683 to 692.
He served as Cameroon's first prime minister and then its first president from 1960 to 1982, knitting the French- and English-speaking halves into one state — who is it?

Ahmadou Ahidjo: President of Cameroon from 1960 to 1982. Ahmadou Babatoura Ahidjo (24 August 1924 – 30 November 1989) was a Cameroonian politician who was the first president of Cameroon from 1960 until 1982.

Ayman al-Zawahiri: Egyptian Islamist militant and physician (1951–2022)

Bayard Rustin: American civil rights activist (1912–1987)

Bohemian Rhapsody: 1975 single by Queen. "Bohemian Rhapsody" is a song by the British rock band Queen, released as the lead single from their fourth studio album, A Night at the Opera (1975).

This German jurist joined the Nazi Party in 1933 and used his legal theories to provide ideological justification for the regime, though he fell out of favor with senior officials by 1936 — who is he?
Carl Schmitt: German jurist and political theorist (1888–1985)
This ferryman of Greek mythology transported souls across the river bordering the underworld, demanding a coin as payment, and even once carried living heroes like Heracles across. Who is he?

Charon: Ferryman of Hades in Greek mythology. In Greek mythology, Charon or Kharon (KAIR-on, -⁠ən; Ancient Greek: Χάρων Ancient Greek pronunciation: [kʰá.rɔːn]) is the ferryman of the Greek underworld.

Taking office at age 35, this president became his country's youngest elected leader after Ecuador's National Assembly was dissolved via a constitutional mechanism in 2023 — who is he?

The first woman to become president of Peru, she took office in December 2022 after her predecessor's failed attempt to dissolve Congress, and was herself removed from power in 2025 — who is she?
Dina Boluarte: President of Peru from 2022 to 2025. Boluarte aligned herself with the right-wing majority of the Peruvian Congress, and received support from the Peruvian Armed Forces.
A grandson of Alfred the Great, this 10th-century King of the English took the throne in 939 and met an abrupt end in a brawl with an outlaw at Pucklechurch — who was he?
Edmund I: King of the English from 939 to 946.
Selected in 1866 to marry the future King Gojong, this consort — known in her lifetime as Queen Min — saw her own clan push the regent, her father-in-law, out of power. Who was she?
Empress Myeongseong: Regent of Joseon from 1873 to 1895.

Claiming to be Ivan the Terrible's youngest son, who had supposedly died in a failed 1591 assassination attempt, this imposter ruled as Tsar of Russia for eleven months before being killed in 1606 — who was he?
False Dmitry I: Tsar of Russia from 1605 to 1606.
Fired from his Army astronomer post in 1957 during the Lavender Scare, this man turned his dismissal into a landmark fight that helped ignite a more militant gay rights movement. Who was he?
Frank Kameny: American gay rights activist (1925–2011)
Born in Rostock and later a Prussian field marshal, this military leader helped defeat Napoleon at the Battle of Leipzig in 1813 and again at Waterloo in 1815 — who is he?
Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher: Prussian field marshal (1742–1819)
According to Exodus, the Israelites made this idol of a young bovine while Moses was away on Mount Sinai — what was it?
Golden calf: Idol in the Torah, the Bible, and the Quran.

This successful insurrection by enslaved Africans against French colonial rule in Saint-Domingue climaxed with independence on New Year's Day, 1804, led by the general Toussaint Louverture — what was it called?
Haitian Revolution: 1791–1804 slave revolt in Hispanola.

Said by ancient tradition to have discovered the True Cross during a religious tour of Jerusalem, this Greek-born Augusta was canonized a saint by both the Catholic and Orthodox churches — who was she?
Helena, mother of Constantine I: Roman empress and saint (c. 246–c. 330)
Loyal to the Polish government-in-exile in London, this WWII underground resistance force swelled to as many as 600,000 fighters against German occupation — which organization?
Home Army: World War II Polish resistance movement.
Born to a Kakwa father and Lugbara mother, this man joined the King's African Rifles in 1946 as a cook before seizing power as Uganda's third president in a 1971 coup — who was he?
Idi Amin: President of Uganda from 1971 to 1979.

Formed in 1946 by former supporters of Benito Mussolini's Republican Fascist Party, which political party became postwar Italy's fourth-largest by the early 1960s while presenting itself as the defender of fascism's legacy?
Italian Social Movement: Neo-fascist political party, 1946–1955.

Formed in 2003 through a merger of several socialist factions and mentored by veteran leader George Fernandes, this Indian party won 12 seats in the 2024 general election as part of the BJP-led coalition. Which party?
Janata Dal (United): Political party in India.

After co-founding a coal brokerage company, this West Virginia politician served as governor before spending 15 years in the U.S. Senate, ultimately leaving the Democratic Party to become an independent in 2024 — who is he?
Joe Manchin: American politician and businessman (born 1947)
This Hong Kong pro-democracy activist rose to global fame during the 2014 Umbrella Movement, landing on Time's Most Influential Teens list and Fortune's "world's greatest leaders" — who is he?

This ancient Indian concept refers to a principle of cause and effect in which intent and actions influence one's future, shaping rebirths and spiritual outcomes — what is this philosophical principle?
Karma: Concept about individuals' intent and actions influencing those individuals' future.
Founded in 910 when Asturian princes moved their capital to a new city in northwestern Iberia, this medieval Christian realm battled the Moors and Vikings to survive — which realm?
Kingdom of León: Country on the Iberian Peninsula (910–1230)
Restored to life four days after death by Jesus in the Gospel of John, this New Testament figure's name is now used to describe any apparent return from the brink of death — who is he?
Lazarus of Bethany: Person resurrected by Jesus in the Gospel of John.
Nicknamed 'the Magnificent,' this unofficial ruler of the Florentine Republic patronized Botticelli and Michelangelo and survived a plot known as the Pazzi conspiracy in 1478 — who is he?
Lorenzo de' Medici: Lord of Florence from 1469 to 1492.

Serving as prime minister in two separate stints, 1981–2003 and 2018–2020, that totaled 24 years, this Malaysian leader was dubbed the "Father of Modernisation" and, at 101, is the world's second-oldest living former head of state — who is he?
Mahathir Mohamad: Prime Minister of Malaysia (1981–2003, 2018–2020). Born and raised in Alor Setar, Kedah, Mahathir excelled at school and became a physician.
The only woman to rule the Habsburg monarchy in her own right, she began a 40-year reign in 1740 over Austria, Hungary, Bohemia and a long list of crowns — who was she?
Maria Theresa: Habsburg monarch from 1740 to 1780.

Rising from humble beginnings in what a former Indian prime minister called a 'miracle of democracy,' this politician became India's first female Scheduled Caste chief minister, leading Uttar Pradesh multiple times — who is she?
Mayawati: 18th Chief Minister of Uttar Pradesh. Mayawati had also served as a Member of Parliament, Rajya Sabha from 2012 to 2017 from Uttar Pradesh.
Better known by his nom de guerre 'Givi,' this pro-Russian separatist commander of the Donetsk People's Republic's Somalia Battalion was assassinated in February 2017 — who was he?
Mikhail Tolstykh: Ukrainian separatist military commander.
As one of the last twelve absolute monarchs in the world, this king renamed his country from its colonial-era name to its current one in 2018 — who is he?
Mswati III: King of Eswatini since 1986.
Sparked by a 1967 uprising in a West Bengal village, this decades-long rural rebellion against the Indian government has been waged by communist guerrilla groups since — what is it called?
Naxalite–Maoist insurgency: Indian anti-government conflict since 1967.
Founded by Nayib Bukele in 2017, this party now holds near-unanimous control of El Salvador's Legislative Assembly — which party?
Nuevas Ideas: Political party in El Salvador. Nuevas Ideas (English: New Ideas; abbreviated N or NI) is the current ruling political party of El Salvador.

Nicknamed "Die Groot Krokodil" — the Big Crocodile — for his tough stance, this hardline Afrikaner was South Africa's last prime minister and first executive State President during apartheid. Who was he?
P. W. Botha: South African politician (1916–2006)
Established in 1946 as the national army of the short-lived Mahabad republic, these are today the internal security forces of Iraq's Kurdistan Region — what are they called?

Peshmerga: Internal security forces of Iraq's Kurdistan Region. The Peshmerga (Kurdish: پێشمەرگه, romanized: Pêşmerge, lit. ''Those Who Face Death'') are the internal security forces of the Kurdistan Region.

Held every June in many cities to commemorate the 1969 Stonewall riots, this annual LGBTQ celebration of rights and self-acceptance began as marches in Chicago, New York, LA, and San Francisco in 1970 — what's it called?
Pride parade: LGBTQ celebration event. The events sometimes also serve as demonstrations for legal rights such as same-sex marriage.
Dubbed a 'warrior Pharaoh,' this Twentieth Dynasty ruler is credited with defeating the invading 'Sea Peoples' and slowing Egypt's decline — who is he?
Ramesses III: Pharaoh of Egypt from 1186 to 1155 BC.

Rutherford B. Hayes: President of the United States from 1877 to 1881.

Sargon II: King of the Neo-Assyrian Empire. Over the course of his seventeen-year reign, Sargon substantially expanded Assyrian territory and enacted important political and military reforms.
In 1902, this Indian princely ruler issued one of India's earliest affirmative-action orders, reserving half of government jobs and education for backward classes — who was he?
Shahu of Kolhapur: Indian ruler and social reformer (1894 to 1922)

In February 1979, Chinese forces launched a surprise invasion of their southern neighbor in retaliation for its overthrow of the Khmer Rouge in Cambodia, withdrawing after about a month — what was this clash called?
Sino-Vietnamese War: War between China and Vietnam in 1979.
Released from Dutch detention by invading Japanese forces in WWII, this nationalist leader went on to become the very first president of his newly independent nation. Who is he?
Sukarno: President of Indonesia from 1945 to 1967.
This brief conflict ran from June 27 to July 7, 1991, ending when the Brioni Accords settled Slovenia's break from Yugoslavia — what was it called?

Ten-Day War: 1991 Slovenia-Yugoslavia conflict. It was fought between the Slovenian Territorial Defence and the Slovenian National Police Force on one side, and the Yugoslav People's Army on the other.
Roughly 2,208 passengers and crew were aboard RMS Titanic when she sank. Approximately how many of them died?
Of the 2,208 passengers and crew aboard, approximately 1,500 died, making it one of the deadliest peacetime sinkings of a single ship.
Head of state for nearly 26 years and often called an autocrat, this longest-serving Finnish president steered a policy of "active neutrality." Who was he?
Urho Kekkonen: President of Finland from 1956 to 1982.
Canonized as a saint by both the Catholic and Orthodox churches, this Rurik dynasty ruler seized Kiev with a Varangian army in 978 after his brothers' deadly feud — who is he?
Vladimir the Great: Grand Prince of Kiev from 978 to 1015.

After nine years as a CIA clandestine officer, this politician represented a sprawling 550-mile Texas border district in Congress before mounting a brief 2024 presidential bid and endorsing Nikki Haley — who is he?
Born in the Khan Yunis refugee camp and educated at the Islamic University of Gaza, he rose to lead Hamas in Gaza before being killed in a 2024 clash with the IDF — who was he?
Yahya Sinwar: Palestinian militant and politician (1962–2024)
Before becoming Colombia's 32nd president in 2002, this leader of the right-wing Democratic Center party served as mayor of Medellín, then governor of Antioquia — who is he?
Álvaro Uribe: President of Colombia from 2002 to 2010.

Oliver Heaviside (born 1850) is the earliest of the four. Although at odds with the scientific establishment for most of his life, Heaviside changed the face of telecommunications, mathematics, and science.
Which of these four is the eldest?
Henrietta Swan Leavitt (born 1868) is the earliest of the four. Henrietta Swan Leavitt (July 4, 1868 – December 12, 1921) was an American astronomer.
Which of these four came first?
C++ (founded 1983) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four was released earliest?
Pascal (programming language) (published 1972) is the earliest of the four.
Pick the mathematician from these four.
Gerardus Mercator is a mathematician. Gerardus Mercator (5 March 1512 – 2 December 1594) was a Flemish geographer, cosmographer and cartographer.
What is the atomic number of Technetium?
Technetium is a chemical element; it has symbol Tc and atomic number 43.
What is the atomic number of Sulfur?
Sulfur (American spelling or sulphur (Commonwealth spelling) is a chemical element; it has symbol S and atomic number 16.
In what year was Niels Bohr born?
Niels Bohr: Although the Bohr model has been supplanted by other models, its underlying principles remain valid.
In what year was Citric acid discovered?
Citric acid is an organic compound with the formula C6H8O7.
In what year was Gold discovered?
Gold is a chemical element; its chemical symbol is Au (from Latin aurum) and atomic number 79.
Methylprednisolone: Pfizer. It is either used at low doses for chronic illnesses or used at high doses during acute flares.
In which country is British Aerospace 146?
British Aerospace 146: United Kingdom. Production figures include the Avro RJ, an improved version from Avro International Aerospace, a subsidiary of BAE Systems.
Who is credited with discovering Rutherfordium?
Rutherfordium: Albert Ghiorso. Rutherfordium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Rf and atomic number 104.
Who is credited with discovering Ampère's force law?
Ampère's force law: André-Marie Ampère. In magnetostatics, Ampère's force law describes the force of attraction or repulsion between two current-carrying wires.
Who is credited with discovering Rhenium?
Rhenium: Walter Noddack. Rhenium is a chemical element; it has symbol Re and atomic number 75.
This tsetse-fly-borne parasitic infection, caused by a protozoan, disproportionately affects humans and cattle across Africa — what is it?
Atrocities in the Congo Free State

African trypanosomiasis is an insect-borne parasitic infection of humans and other animals caused by the protozoan species Trypanosoma brucei, which is transmitted by the bite of an infected tsetse fly.
This group of large, semiaquatic boas native to tropical South America includes the green species, among the largest snakes on Earth — name the group?
Anaconda are a group of large boas of the genus Eunectes.
Considered a visual art even though it leans on civil engineering, this discipline gives us cultural symbols that often outlast the civilizations that built them. What is it?
Architecture is the study and practice of designing structures, especially habitable ones.

Originating in Central Africa and classified as a hound by the American Kennel Club, this dog breed doesn't bark but instead makes an unusual yodel-like sound due to its uniquely shaped larynx — what's the breed?
Basenji is a breed of hunting dog created from stock that originated in Central Africa, including in the Republic of the Congo and other adjacent tropical African countries.
This small bird in the Old World flycatcher family breeds among rocky habitats from the British Isles to Morocco and east to central China — what species is it?
Black redstart (Phoenicurus ochruros) is a small passerine bird in the Old World flycatcher family.

Forced to flee Italy in 1938 under the racial laws, this experimental physicist had earlier invented an improved coincidence circuit and traveled to Eritrea to show cosmic rays arrived more strongly from the West than the East — who was he?
Bruno Rossi (13 April 1905 - 21 November 1993) was an Italian-American experimental physicist.

Honored twice by the American Psychological Association — in 1956 for scientific contributions and 1972 for professional ones — this psychologist championed a person-centered approach to therapy — who is he?
Carl Rogers (January 8, 1902 - February 4, 1987) was an American psychologist who was one of the founders of humanistic psychology and was known especially for his person-centered psychotherapy.
This plant-cell organelle uses chlorophyll pigments to capture sunlight and convert it into chemical energy, ultimately producing sugar via the Calvin cycle — what is it?
Chloroplast (-plahst) is a type of organelle known as a plastid that conducts photosynthesis mostly in plant and algal cells.

Ranging across most of Europe and into the Palearctic as far as northwestern China, this medium-sized bird of prey sees its northernmost populations migrate as far as South Africa each winter — which raptor?
Common buzzard (Buteo buteo) is a medium-sized bird of prey with a large range.

Caused by prolonged exposure to glucocorticoids like cortisol, this collection of symptoms includes abdominal weight gain with thin limbs, a rounded red face, and weak, fragile skin that heals poorly — what's it called?
Cushing's syndrome is a collection of signs and symptoms due to prolonged exposure to glucocorticoids such as cortisol.

This gut ailment flares up when small pouches in the wall of the large intestine become inflamed, often striking with sudden lower-abdominal pain — fever or bloody stool warns of a complication; what is it?
Diverticulitis is a gastrointestinal disease characterized by inflammation of abnormal pouches - diverticula - that can develop in the wall of the large intestine.
Many of these Northern Hemisphere shade trees, prized along old European and American streets, were wiped out by a fungus carried by bark beetles — which tree genus is this?
Elm are deciduous and semi-deciduous trees comprising the genus Ulmus in the family Ulmaceae.
First confirmed around a pulsar in 1992, this astronomical term describes any planet located outside our own solar system — over 6,300 have now been confirmed — what is it called?
Exoplanet is a planet outside the Solar System. The first confirmed detection of an exoplanet was in 1992 around a pulsar, and the first detection around a main-sequence star was in 1995.
This West Point graduate, eighth in his class of 670, commanded Apollo 8's historic flight around the Moon in 1968 — who is he?
Frank Borman (March 14, 1928 - November 7, 2023) was an American United States Air Force (USAF) colonel, aeronautical engineer, NASA astronaut, test pilot, and businessman.
Built from glutamate, cysteine and glycine, this tripeptide is the most abundant low-molecular-mass thiol in most cells and a key antioxidant guarding against free radicals — what is it?
Glutathione (GSH) is a tripeptide made of the amino acids glutamate, cysteine, and glycine.

In 1896 this English physician dosed himself with mescaline and wrote one of the first public reports of the trip; he also co-wrote English's first medical textbook on homosexuality and coined the term 'narcissism' — who was he?
Havelock Ellis (2 February 1859 - 8 July 1939) was an English physician, eugenicist, writer, progressive intellectual and social reformer who studied human sexuality.
Found from Alaska to Tierra del Fuego across roughly 375 species, the males of this American bird family boast the most diverse plumage colors of any birds — what are they?
Hummingbird are birds native to the Americas and comprise the biological family Trochilidae.
An ISO standard defines it as "a new or changed entity, realizing or redistributing value" — and it's related to, but not the same as, invention. What word are we after?
Innovation is the practical implementation of ideas that result in the creation or improvements of goods or services.
This psychologist edited 'Psychological Review' from 1910 to 1915 and was later ranked the 17th most-cited psychologist of the 20th century for popularizing behaviorism — who is he?
John B. Watson (January 9, 1878 - September 25, 1958) was an American psychologist who popularized the scientific theory of behaviorism, establishing it as a psychological school.
This unit of speed equals exactly one nautical mile per hour, roughly 1.15 mph, and is the standard measure used in maritime and aviation contexts — what is it called?
Knot (unit) is a unit of speed equal to one nautical mile per hour, exactly 1.852 km/h (approximately 1.151 mph or 0.514 m/s).
Also called the great grey slug, this 10-20cm mollusc has a strange courtship where mating pairs suspend themselves in midair from a mucus thread — what species is it?
Limax maximus (literally, "biggest slug"), known by the common names great grey slug and leopard slug, is a species of slug in the family Limacidae, the keeled slugs.

Resembling some toxic look-alikes despite being a well-regarded edible, this basidiomycete fungus is a fairly common species on well-drained soils across temperate Eurasia, found solitary or in fairy rings in pastures — name the species?
Macrolepiota procera is a basidiomycete fungus with a large, prominent fruiting body resembling a parasol.
First synthesized in 1982 near Darmstadt, this fleeting synthetic element of the periodic table's seventh period was named in 1997 after a pioneering Austrian-Swedish nuclear physicist. What is it?
Meitnerium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Mt and atomic number 109.
This small, subterranean mammal has velvety fur, tiny eyes, and short powerful forelimbs with oversized paws built for constant digging — what animal is it?
In this category of over 80 recognized conditions, the body's adaptive immune system mistakenly attacks its own healthy tissue as though it were foreign. What is it?

Navel (clinically known as the umbilicus; pl.: umbilici or umbilicuses; also known as the belly button or tummy button) is a protruding, flat, or hollowed area on the abdomen at the attachment site of the umbilical cord.
This insect order includes dragonflies and damselflies, the bulkier ones holding wings out at rest while the slender ones fold theirs along the body — what is it?
Odonata is an order of predatory flying insects that includes the dragonflies and damselflies (as well as the Epiophlebia damsel-dragonflies).
Usually numbering four and tucked behind the thyroid, these small endocrine structures release a hormone that kicks in when blood calcium runs low — which structures?
Parathyroid gland are small endocrine glands in the neck of humans and other tetrapods.
What dissociative anesthetic, known on the street as a recreational drug, can cause hallucinations, paranoia, and psychotic behavior, and is often smoked or mixed with cannabis or tobacco?
Phencyclidine (PCP), also known in its use as a street drug as angel dust among other names, is a dissociative anesthetic mainly used recreationally for its significant mind-altering effects.
Named after the American diplomat who introduced it to the US in the 1820s, this red-and-green plant native to Mexico is a Christmas staple — what plant is it?
Poinsettia (Euphorbia pulcherrima) is a commercially important flowering plant species of the diverse spurge family Euphorbiaceae.
Split into roughly a dozen Afrotropical species and around 167 Neotropical species — among them the blue-and-yellow macaw and the grey parrot — which bird family is this?
Psittacidae is one of three families of true parrots.
What dimensionless quantity in fluid dynamics, expressing the ratio of inertial to viscous forces, determines whether a flow will be smooth and laminar or chaotic and turbulent?
Reynolds number (Re) is a dimensionless quantity that helps predict fluid flow patterns in different situations by measuring the ratio between inertial and viscous forces.
Named after an American veterinary surgeon, this genus of rod-shaped, gram-negative bacteria includes over 2,650 serotypes within a single major species — name it?
Salmonella is a genus of rod-shaped, (bacillus) Gram-negative bacteria of the family Enterobacteriaceae.

This dog breed from southern China, traditionally kept as a property guardian, was driven to the brink of extinction in the 20th century and is known in the West for its deep wrinkles. What breed is this?

Shar Pei (Cantonese; pinyin: sh p) is a dog breed from
southern China.
This birth defect involves incomplete closure of the spinal column and its surrounding membranes during early pregnancy, occurring in three recognized forms — what condition is it?
Spina bifida (SB; Latin for 'split spine') is a birth defect in which there is incomplete closing of the spine and the membranes around the spinal cord during early development in pregnancy.
Named for its long, flat, sword-like bill, this large migratory predatory fish loses all its teeth and scales by adulthood and is a popular target among billfish anglers — what is it?
Swordfish (Xiphias gladius), also known as the broadbill in some countries, are large, highly migratory predatory fish characterized by a long, flat, sword-like, pointed bill.

This weakly radioactive silvery metal, atomic number 90, tarnishes olive-grey in air, and its most stable isotope has a half-life of about 14 billion years — roughly the age of the universe. What element is this?
Thorium is a chemical element; it has symbol Th and atomic number 90.
An important food fish found in marine and brackish waters from the Baltic to the Mediterranean, this flatfish's Black Sea relatives are now classified as a separate species — which fish?
Turbot is a relatively large species of flatfish in the family Scophthalmidae.
What's the name for the small, non-cancerous skin growths caused by the human papillomavirus, most common on the hands and feet but also appearing as genital or filiform forms?
Wart are non-cancerous viral growths usually occurring on the hands and feet but which can also affect other locations, such as the genitals or face.

This paraphilia describes a sexual fixation on non-human animals, distinct from acting on such attraction, and was estimated in one 2021 study to affect about 2 percent of the population — name the term?
Zoophilia is a paraphilia in which a person experiences a sexual fixation on non-human animals.
Regarded as one of Formula One's greatest engineers, his car designs have won 14 Drivers' and 12 Constructors' Championships across three decades?
Adrian Newey: British engineer, aerodynamicist and motorsport executive (born 1958)
This Swedish chemist held 355 patents, invented dynamite, and then left his fortune to fund a famous set of prizes. Who was he?
Alfred Nobel: Swedish chemist and inventor (1833–1896)

Inspired by Ørsted's 1820 discovery that current creates a magnetic field, this principle relating a magnetic field's circulation to the current passing through a loop was later generalized by Maxwell with a displacement current term — which physics principle?
Ampère's circuital law: Concept in classical electromagnetism.

A political economy professor turned finance minister after a 1926 coup, this Portuguese dictator ruled his corporatist 'New State' from 1932 until 1968, in one of modern Europe's longest authoritarian regimes — who is he?
António de Oliveira Salazar: Prime Minister of Portugal from 1932 to 1968.

Also known by a folksy nickname, this small North American tree produces a custard-textured fruit tasting like banana or pineapple — despite containing a neurotoxin elsewhere in the plant. What species is it?
Asimina triloba: Species of tree. Asimina triloba, the American papaw, pawpaw, paw paw, or paw-paw, among many regional names, is a species of small deciduous tree.
A Kenyan economist who met his future wife at the University of Hawaii, this man became the father of a future U.S. president and the subject of that son's 1995 memoir — who is he?
Before becoming TV's most famous bow-tied science educator, this Boeing mechanical engineer invented a hydraulic resonance suppressor tube for 747s, then quit to do sketch comedy. Who is he?
Developed alongside the 707 airliner from the same prototype, this narrower, shorter jet became the U.S. Air Force's first jet-powered refueling tanker in 1957 — name the aircraft?
Boeing KC-135 Stratotanker: US military aerial refueling and transport aircraft.
Sold under the brand name Pulmicort, this steroid drug treats asthma when inhaled but also comes as a nasal spray for allergies and a rectal foam for bowel disease — which medication?
This highly contagious virus, spread through feces, can kill up to 91% of untreated dogs and wolves and also strikes foxes, cats, and skunks — what is it?
Canine parvovirus: Contagious virus mainly affecting dogs.
Native to Madagascar, this flowering plant known as the Madagascar periwinkle is the source of two major cancer-fighting drugs — what is it?
Catharanthus roseus: Species of flowering plant in the family Apocynaceae.
Caused by a member of the herpesvirus family, this airborne illness usually starts on the chest, back, and face before the itchy little blisters scab over all over the body — what is it?
Sold under the brand name Klonopin, this long-acting benzodiazepine kicks in within an hour and lasts eight to twelve, treating anxiety, seizures, and panic — which drug is it?
Clonazepam: Benzodiazepine medication. It possesses anxiolytic, anticonvulsant, sedative, hypnotic, and skeletal muscle relaxant properties.

Nicknamed the deaf adder or long-cripple in parts of Europe, this legless, burrowing lizard has smooth scales that don't overlap — and despite its name, it's neither a snake nor what it sounds like. What is it?
Common slow worm: Species of legless lizard. The common slow worm (Anguis fragilis) is a non-venomous species of legless lizard native to Europe.
Found in the tropics of Africa, Asia, the Americas, and Australia, this large semiaquatic reptile congregates in rivers and wetlands and is closely related to alligators and caimans — what is it?
Crocodile: Family of large reptilian carnivores.
This Manhattan Project physicist later led the Federation of American Scientists and is best remembered for his 1959 Senate testimony opposing Lewis Strauss's Commerce nomination — who is he?
David L. Hill: American nuclear physicist (1919–2008)
Named for the unique double-beamed bones under its tail, this long-necked Jurassic giant is one of the most common fossils found in North America's Morrison Formation. What dinosaur is it?
Diplodocus: Genus of diplodocid sauropod dinosaurs (fossil)
Starting life bilaterally symmetrical as larvae but growing into five-pointed radial adults, this animal phylum includes starfish, sea urchins, and sea cucumbers — what is it called?
Echinoderm: Marine phylum of animals often with radial symmetries.
This branch of zoology, whose name derives from Greek words for 'insect' and 'study,' covers a field that has described over 1.3 million species — which discipline?
The only Old World member of its family to breed in the Northern Hemisphere's temperate zones, this migratory songbird winters in central and southern Africa — what is it?
Eurasian golden oriole: Species of bird.
This Swiss thinker, alongside Charles Sanders Peirce, is considered one of the two founders of semiotics — the field he himself called 'semiology' — who is he?
Ferdinand de Saussure: Swiss linguist and philosopher (1857–1913)
Marked by physical traits such as a long face, large ears, and unusually flexible fingers, this inherited neurodevelopmental disorder stems from a repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene — which condition?
Fragile X syndrome: X-linked dominant genetic disorder.
This is the largest lizard family, boasting over 950 species that cling to surfaces via Van der Waals forces in their toe hairs — including house, tokay, and day varieties — which family?
Gekkonidae: Family of lizards. Gekkonidae (the common geckos) is the largest family of geckos, containing over 950 described species in 62 genera.
Caused by iodine deficiency in over 90% of cases worldwide, this neck swelling results from an enlarged thyroid gland — what's the condition called?
Goitre: Neck swelling due to enlarged thyroid gland. A goitre (British English, spelled goiter in American English) is a swelling in the neck resulting from an enlarged thyroid gland.

This French civil engineer made his name building railway bridges like the Garabit Viaduct and later helped erect the Statue of Liberty, before retiring to study meteorology and aerodynamics — who was he?
This Dutch-born entrepreneur produced Japan's first major turn-based role-playing game and later secured the console distribution rights to a Russian puzzle game called Tetris — who is he?
Henk Rogers: Dutch-born American computer programmer (born 1953)
Despite the name, this 'living fossil' is no crustacean at all — it's a chelicerate, kin to spiders and scorpions, and its three-part body ends in a spiky tail called a telson. What creature is it?
Horseshoe crab: Family of basal chelicerates.
This physical phenomenon describes how a system's current state depends on its past history, forming looping curves in magnets and giving hard disk drives their memory — what is it?
Hysteresis: Dependence of the state of a system on its history. Hysteresis can be found in physics, chemistry, engineering, biology, and economics.
This condition restricts blood flow to tissue, starving cells of oxygen and nutrients due to causes like thrombosis or embolism — what's it called?
Ischemia: Restriction in blood supply to tissues.
As Grand Pensionary of Holland during the Dutch Golden Age, this statesman dominated politics from 1650 until the 'Disaster Year' of 1672 — who was he?

A NASA mathematician and human computer, she calculated the orbital mechanics critical to America's first crewed spaceflights and was among the first African-American women to work as a NASA scientist — who was she?
Native to the Mediterranean and used to season food as a bay leaf, this aromatic evergreen prominent in classical Greco-Roman culture can grow up to 20 metres tall — what is its scientific name?
Laurus nobilis: Species of flowering plant in the laurel family Lauraceae.
Soft, movable, and painless, this benign fatty-tissue growth most often shows up under the skin on the upper back, shoulders, or abdomen — what is it?
Lipoma: Benign tumor made of fat tissue.
This common, nonspecific medical sign involves lymph nodes becoming abnormally swollen or enlarged, with causes ranging from the common cold to cancer. What's the condition called?
Lymphadenopathy: Abnormal change in size of the lymph nodes.
A student of Marie Curie, this French physicist discovered the element francium in 1939 and later became the first woman elected to the French Académie des Sciences — who was she?

Encompassing conditions marked by a clinically significant disturbance in thinking, emotional regulation, or behavior that causes real distress or impaired functioning, this broad psychiatric category has causes that remain often unclear — what is the umbrella term for it?
NATO nicknames it 'Foxhound,' and at roughly 3,000 km/h it's the fastest operational combat aircraft known — which interceptor, a Soviet successor to the MiG-25, is it?
Mikoyan MiG-31: Interceptor aircraft. The MiG-31 is the fastest known operational combat aircraft, with a top speed around 3,000 km/h (1,600 knots).

Synthesized in 2003 at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research in Dubna and named in 2016 for the Russian region around it, this element 115 has a most-stable isotope lasting just 0.65 seconds — what is it?
Moscovium: Chemical element with atomic number 115 (Mc)

As modern science emerged, this concept came to mean the passive reality moved by divine laws — and after the Industrial Revolution, the part of the world untouched by intentional human hands. What word is it?
Nature: Material world and its phenomena.
Nicknamed the 'winter vomiting disease' and spread by the fecal-oral route, this is the most common cause of gastroenteritis — what is it?
Norovirus: Type of viruses that cause gastroenteritis.
Named after an ancient Greek city, this cactus genus is better known by its fruit's common name, the prickly pear, and goes by nopal or sabra in other cultures — what genus is it?
Opuntia: Genus of cactus. The plant has been introduced to Australia, southern Europe, the Middle East, and parts of Africa.
One researcher catalogued as many as 549 varieties of this psychological category, defined by intense arousal toward things that aren't sexual by nature — what is the term?
This serous membrane lines the abdominal cavity and serves as a conduit for the blood vessels and nerves of the organs it covers — what is it called?
Peritoneum: Membrane that forms lining of abdominal cavity or coelom.

A counting argument in mathematics: if you have more items than containers, at least one container must hold more than one item. Famous example: three gloves, but only two hand categories — what's this principle?
Pigeonhole principle: If there are more items than boxes holding them, one box must contain at least two items.
Looking like a jellyfish but actually a floating colony of cooperating zooids, this venomous siphonophore is also nicknamed the bluebottle — what is it?
Portuguese man o' war: Species of marine cnidarian.

This noncontagious autoimmune disease shows up as dry, scaly red or purple patches, and injuring the skin can trigger new lesions right at that spot — a quirk called the Koebner phenomenon — what is it?
Psoriasis: Autoimmune diseases of the skin. Psoriasis is a long-lasting, noncontagious autoimmune disease characterized by patches of abnormal skin.

Born Richard Alpert, this spiritual teacher researched psychedelics with Timothy Leary at Harvard before writing the 1971 bestseller Be Here Now, popularizing Eastern spirituality in the West. What name did he later take?
As chairman of Purdue Pharma, this physician-businessman oversaw the launch of OxyContin and was later portrayed in the miniseries Dopesick and Painkiller — who is he?
Also called false saffron, this thistle-like annual is one of the world's oldest crops, prized today for the vegetable oil pressed from its seeds — what plant is it?
Safflower: Species of plant. Safflower (Carthamus tinctorius), also false saffron, is a highly branched, herbaceous, thistle-like annual plant in the family Asteraceae.
Co-founder of the file-sharing service Napster, this entrepreneur became Facebook's first president before later founding a philanthropic foundation focused on life sciences — who is he?
Sean Parker: American entrepreneur and philanthropist (born 1979)

This Irish mathematician and physicist held Cambridge's Lucasian Professorship for an unmatched 54 years, leaving his name on equations of fluid mechanics and a theorem of vector calculus — who is it?
Sir George Stokes, 1st Baronet: British mathematician and physicist (1819–1903)
This family of roughly 1,450 moths flies so swiftly on narrow wings and streamlined bodies that some species hover at flowers and are routinely mistaken for hummingbirds — what's its scientific name?
Sphingidae: Family of insects. The Sphingidae are a family of moths commonly called sphinx moths, also colloquially known as hawk moths, with many of their caterpillars known as hornworms.

Distinct from addiction, this biopsychological condition occurs when a person's body has adapted so much to a psychoactive drug that stopping triggers withdrawal, requiring continued use just to function — what is this condition called?
Substance dependence: Need for a drug, whose discontinuation results in withdrawal symptoms.
One of the largest parasitoid wasps, this creature paralyzes its eight-legged prey with a sting, drags it into a nest, and lays a single egg so the larva can devour the still-living host. What is it?
Tarantula hawk: Common name for two genera of wasps.
Best known for his 1651 work 'Leviathan' and its influential take on social contract theory, this English philosopher once met Galileo while tutoring the Cavendish family across Europe — who was he?
Thomas Hobbes: English philosopher and political theorist (1588–1679)
Only about 76 to 90 nucleotides long, this adaptor molecule reads each three-letter mRNA codon with a matching anticodon and ferries the right amino acid to the ribosome — what is it?
Transfer RNA: RNA that facilitates the addition of amino acids to a new protein.
Element 121, this not-yet-synthesized superactinide is expected to open a brand-new g-block of the periodic table and may sit on the 'island of stability' — what's its placeholder name?
Unbiunium: Theoretical chemical element with atomic number 121 (Ubu)
Running a boutique called Sex with partner Malcolm McLaren, this English designer helped bring punk fashion into the mainstream and shaped the look of the Sex Pistols — who is she?
A short-legged, stubby-tailed marsupial native to Australia, this burrowing animal can weigh up to 35 kilograms and survives in an isolated pocket of central Queensland — which creature?
Wombat: Species of marsupial native to Australia.
Protactinium is denoted by which symbol?
The symbol for protactinium is Pa. Protactinium is a chemical element; it has symbol Pa and atomic number 91.
